1.   Mayor Havemeyer was a Democrat who ran as a Republican against the Democratic Tweed Ring in 1872.  
2.   Acting Mayors Coman, Vance, Kline and Collins did not seek election as mayor.  
3.   Acting Mayors McKee and Impellitteri were Democrats who lost the Democratic primary to succeed themselves, but still ran in the general election as independents.  
4.   Elected Mayor Oakey Hall won re-election, while Mayor Wickham did not seek it. Mayors Mitchel and O'Brien lost attempts at re-election, while Mayor Impellitteri did not run for a full term in the 1953 regular general election after losing the Democratic primary.
Brooklyn elected a mayor from 1834 until its consolidation into the City of Greater New York in 1898, whose own second mayor, Seth Low, had been mayor of Brooklyn from 1881 to 1885. Since 1898, Brooklyn has, in place of a separate mayor, elected a borough president.
Long Island City, now a neighborhood within the borough of Queens, was incorporated as a city on May 4, 1870 and was consolidated into the present City of Greater New York on January 1, 1898, along with the city of Brooklyn and several other municipalities in the counties of Queens and Richmond.

**William R. Grace**was an American shipowner and founder of W.R. Grace & Co., a corporation that was for many years a dominant influence on the economy of South America’s west coast and, under the management of his heirs, became a multibillion-dollar conglomerate in the late 20th century.
Grace ran away to New York at the age of 14 but later returned to Ireland. In 1850 he visited Callao, Peru, where he entered the shipping house of Bryce & Co. as a clerk, becoming a partner two years later. Early success came to him when he positioned one of the firm’s supply ships off the Peruvian coast, thereby permitting cargo fleets to purchase supplies without sending their workers ashore. In 1854 the firm became Bryce, Grace & Co. and within a few years controlled much of the shipping along the coasts of Peru and Chile. His health declining, Grace turned the management of the firm over to his brother and left Peru in 1865.

# William R. Grace
In 1868 he organized the shipping firm of W.R. Grace & Co. in New York, serving ports on three continents and in the process winning a substantial portion of the U.S.–South American trade. Grace was the main arms supplier to Peru before and during its unsuccessful war with Chile in 1879–83, and after the war he assumed the country’s staggering war debt. In return, his company received huge concessions from Peru in the form of silver mines, oil and mineral deposits, and guano deposits. His business exploits in the country earned him the moniker “Pirate of Peru.” Grace also invested extensively in commodities and real estate in Peru and Chile and had numerous other business interests both in the United States and abroad. In 1892 he established the first direct steamship service between New York and Peru.
Grace was a major contributor to the Irish famine relief effort in 1880. He became interested in politics and was twice elected mayor of New York, in 1880 and 1884. His advocacy of a shipping canal through Central America met with success with the start of American-led construction of the Panama Canal in 1904.

## **William Russell Grace (1832–1904): Industrialist, Politician, and Philanthropist**
William Russell Grace stands as one of the most influential Irish-American figures of the 19th century—a pioneering industrialist, reformist mayor of New York City, and humanitarian of international renown. Born on May 10, 1832, in Riverstown near the Cove of Cork, Ireland, Grace was the son of James Grace and Eleanor May Russell (née Ellen). Though his birth occurred while the family was away from home, he was raised on the Grace estate at Ballylinan in Queen’s County (now County Laois), near the town of Athy. The family also resided for a time at Brooklawn House on Love Lane (now Donore Avenue), indicative of their prominent social standing.
In 1846, at the age of 14, young Grace defied his father's wishes and emigrated to New York City, where he labored as a printer’s devil and a shoemaker’s helper before briefly returning to Ireland in 1848. He later attended Belvedere College in Dublin but left before completing his studies.
In 1851, William and his father journeyed to Callao, Peru, with the ambitious aim of establishing an Irish agricultural colony. While James Grace returned to Ireland, William remained in Peru, where he entered the service of the shipping firm John Bryce & Co. His aptitude for commerce quickly became evident. The firm was restructured as Bryce, Grace & Company in 1854, and later as Grace Brothers & Co. in 1865. By the 1870s, it became _W. R. Grace and Company_, which would grow into a global enterprise with enduring influence in shipping, chemicals, and finance.

## **William Russell Grace (1832–1904): Industrialist, Politician, and Philanthropist**
Grace’s rise in the mercantile world was matched by a notable political career. In 1880, he made history as the first Roman Catholic—and the first Irish-American—to be elected mayor of New York City, running as an opponent of the corrupt Tammany Hall political machine. His administration was marked by a commitment to civic reform: he rooted out police corruption, curtailed patronage networks, cracked down on organized vice, and successfully opposed the Louisiana Lottery. Although defeated in the subsequent election, he returned triumphantly to office in 1884 on an Independent ticket. During his second term, Grace had the honor of formally receiving the Statue of Liberty from France, a symbolic moment in the city’s and nation’s immigrant narrative.
Outside of politics and business, Grace was an exemplary philanthropist. Following the Irish Famine of 1879, he played a leading role in relief efforts, personally underwriting nearly a quarter of the aid sent aboard the _USS Constellation_ to Ireland. In 1897, he and his brother, Michael Grace, co-founded the _Grace Institute_—an enduring institution dedicated to the vocational education of women, particularly immigrants, in New York City.
On September 11, 1859, Grace married Lillius Gilchrist (1839–1922), daughter of George W. Gilchrist, a distinguished shipbuilder of Thomaston, Maine, and Mary Jane Smalley Gilchrist. Together, William and Lillius had eleven children, further cementing the Grace family’s legacy in both American public life and transatlantic history.
William Russell Grace died on March 21, 1904. His life and career encapsulate the story of 19th-century America itself—immigration, enterprise, public service, and philanthropy—and his legacy continues through the institutions he built and the ideals he championed.

# William R. Grace
In 1868 he organized the shipping firm of W.R. Grace & Co. in New York, serving ports on three continents and in the process winning a substantial portion of the U.S.–South American trade. Grace was the main arms supplier to Peru before and during its unsuccessful war with Chile in 1879–83, and after the war he assumed the country’s staggering war debt. In return, his company received huge concessions from Peru in the form of silver mines, oil and mineral deposits, and guano deposits. His business exploits in the country earned him the moniker “Pirate of Peru.” Grace also invested extensively in commodities and real estate in Peru and Chile and had numerous other business interests both in the United States and abroad. In 1892 he established the first direct steamship service between New York and Peru.
Grace was a major contributor to the Irish famine relief effort in 1880. He became interested in politics and was twice elected mayor of New York, in 1880 and 1884. His advocacy of a shipping canal through Central America met with success with the start of American-led construction of the Panama Canal in 1904.

## **William Russell Grace (1832–1904): Industrialist, Politician, and Philanthropist**
William Russell Grace stands as one of the most influential Irish-American figures of the 19th century—a pioneering industrialist, reformist mayor of New York City, and humanitarian of international renown. Born on May 10, 1832, in Riverstown near the Cove of Cork, Ireland, Grace was the son of James Grace and Eleanor May Russell (née Ellen). Though his birth occurred while the family was away from home, he was raised on the Grace estate at Ballylinan in Queen’s County (now County Laois), near the town of Athy. The family also resided for a time at Brooklawn House on Love Lane (now Donore Avenue), indicative of their prominent social standing.
In 1846, at the age of 14, young Grace defied his father's wishes and emigrated to New York City, where he labored as a printer’s devil and a shoemaker’s helper before briefly returning to Ireland in 1848. He later attended Belvedere College in Dublin but left before completing his studies.
In 1851, William and his father journeyed to Callao, Peru, with the ambitious aim of establishing an Irish agricultural colony. While James Grace returned to Ireland, William remained in Peru, where he entered the service of the shipping firm John Bryce & Co. His aptitude for commerce quickly became evident. The firm was restructured as Bryce, Grace & Company in 1854, and later as Grace Brothers & Co. in 1865. By the 1870s, it became _W. R. Grace and Company_, which would grow into a global enterprise with enduring influence in shipping, chemicals, and finance.

## **William Russell Grace (1832–1904): Industrialist, Politician, and Philanthropist**
Grace’s rise in the mercantile world was matched by a notable political career. In 1880, he made history as the first Roman Catholic—and the first Irish-American—to be elected mayor of New York City, running as an opponent of the corrupt Tammany Hall political machine. His administration was marked by a commitment to civic reform: he rooted out police corruption, curtailed patronage networks, cracked down on organized vice, and successfully opposed the Louisiana Lottery. Although defeated in the subsequent election, he returned triumphantly to office in 1884 on an Independent ticket. During his second term, Grace had the honor of formally receiving the Statue of Liberty from France, a symbolic moment in the city’s and nation’s immigrant narrative.
Outside of politics and business, Grace was an exemplary philanthropist. Following the Irish Famine of 1879, he played a leading role in relief efforts, personally underwriting nearly a quarter of the aid sent aboard the _USS Constellation_ to Ireland. In 1897, he and his brother, Michael Grace, co-founded the _Grace Institute_—an enduring institution dedicated to the vocational education of women, particularly immigrants, in New York City.
On September 11, 1859, Grace married Lillius Gilchrist (1839–1922), daughter of George W. Gilchrist, a distinguished shipbuilder of Thomaston, Maine, and Mary Jane Smalley Gilchrist. Together, William and Lillius had eleven children, further cementing the Grace family’s legacy in both American public life and transatlantic history.
William Russell Grace died on March 21, 1904. His life and career encapsulate the story of 19th-century America itself—immigration, enterprise, public service, and philanthropy—and his legacy continues through the institutions he built and the ideals he championed.

## **William Russell Grace (1832–1904): Industrialist, Politician, and Philanthropist**
Grace’s rise in the mercantile world was matched by a notable political career. In 1880, he made history as the first Roman Catholic—and the first Irish-American—to be elected mayor of New York City, running as an opponent of the corrupt Tammany Hall political machine. His administration was marked by a commitment to civic reform: he rooted out police corruption, curtailed patronage networks, cracked down on organized vice, and successfully opposed the Louisiana Lottery. Although defeated in the subsequent election, he returned triumphantly to office in 1884 on an Independent ticket. During his second term, Grace had the honor of formally receiving the Statue of Liberty from France, a symbolic moment in the city’s and nation’s immigrant narrative.
Outside of politics and business, Grace was an exemplary philanthropist. Following the Irish Famine of 1879, he played a leading role in relief efforts, personally underwriting nearly a quarter of the aid sent aboard the _USS Constellation_ to Ireland. In 1897, he and his brother, Michael Grace, co-founded the _Grace Institute_—an enduring institution dedicated to the vocational education of women, particularly immigrants, in New York City.
On September 11, 1859, Grace married Lillius Gilchrist (1839–1922), daughter of George W. Gilchrist, a distinguished shipbuilder of Thomaston, Maine, and Mary Jane Smalley Gilchrist. Together, William and Lillius had eleven children, further cementing the Grace family’s legacy in both American public life and transatlantic history.
William Russell Grace died on March 21, 1904. His life and career encapsulate the story of 19th-century America itself—immigration, enterprise, public service, and philanthropy—and his legacy continues through the institutions he built and the ideals he championed.

**William R. Grace**was an American shipowner and founder of W.R. Grace & Co., a corporation that was for many years a dominant influence on the economy of South America’s west coast and, under the management of his heirs, became a multibillion-dollar conglomerate in the late 20th century.
Grace ran away to New York at the age of 14 but later returned to Ireland. In 1850 he visited Callao, Peru, where he entered the shipping house of Bryce & Co. as a clerk, becoming a partner two years later. Early success came to him when he positioned one of the firm’s supply ships off the Peruvian coast, thereby permitting cargo fleets to purchase supplies without sending their workers ashore. In 1854 the firm became Bryce, Grace & Co. and within a few years controlled much of the shipping along the coasts of Peru and Chile. His health declining, Grace turned the management of the firm over to his brother and left Peru in 1865.

# William R. Grace
In 1868 he organized the shipping firm of W.R. Grace & Co. in New York, serving ports on three continents and in the process winning a substantial portion of the U.S.–South American trade. Grace was the main arms supplier to Peru before and during its unsuccessful war with Chile in 1879–83, and after the war he assumed the country’s staggering war debt. In return, his company received huge concessions from Peru in the form of silver mines, oil and mineral deposits, and guano deposits. His business exploits in the country earned him the moniker “Pirate of Peru.” Grace also invested extensively in commodities and real estate in Peru and Chile and had numerous other business interests both in the United States and abroad. In 1892 he established the first direct steamship service between New York and Peru.
Grace was a major contributor to the Irish famine relief effort in 1880. He became interested in politics and was twice elected mayor of New York, in 1880 and 1884. His advocacy of a shipping canal through Central America met with success with the start of American-led construction of the Panama Canal in 1904.

## **William Russell Grace (1832–1904): Industrialist, Politician, and Philanthropist**
William Russell Grace stands as one of the most influential Irish-American figures of the 19th century—a pioneering industrialist, reformist mayor of New York City, and humanitarian of international renown. Born on May 10, 1832, in Riverstown near the Cove of Cork, Ireland, Grace was the son of James Grace and Eleanor May Russell (née Ellen). Though his birth occurred while the family was away from home, he was raised on the Grace estate at Ballylinan in Queen’s County (now County Laois), near the town of Athy. The family also resided for a time at Brooklawn House on Love Lane (now Donore Avenue), indicative of their prominent social standing.
In 1846, at the age of 14, young Grace defied his father's wishes and emigrated to New York City, where he labored as a printer’s devil and a shoemaker’s helper before briefly returning to Ireland in 1848. He later attended Belvedere College in Dublin but left before completing his studies.
In 1851, William and his father journeyed to Callao, Peru, with the ambitious aim of establishing an Irish agricultural colony. While James Grace returned to Ireland, William remained in Peru, where he entered the service of the shipping firm John Bryce & Co. His aptitude for commerce quickly became evident. The firm was restructured as Bryce, Grace & Company in 1854, and later as Grace Brothers & Co. in 1865. By the 1870s, it became _W. R. Grace and Company_, which would grow into a global enterprise with enduring influence in shipping, chemicals, and finance.

## **William Russell Grace (1832–1904): Industrialist, Politician, and Philanthropist**
Grace’s rise in the mercantile world was matched by a notable political career. In 1880, he made history as the first Roman Catholic—and the first Irish-American—to be elected mayor of New York City, running as an opponent of the corrupt Tammany Hall political machine. His administration was marked by a commitment to civic reform: he rooted out police corruption, curtailed patronage networks, cracked down on organized vice, and successfully opposed the Louisiana Lottery. Although defeated in the subsequent election, he returned triumphantly to office in 1884 on an Independent ticket. During his second term, Grace had the honor of formally receiving the Statue of Liberty from France, a symbolic moment in the city’s and nation’s immigrant narrative.
Outside of politics and business, Grace was an exemplary philanthropist. Following the Irish Famine of 1879, he played a leading role in relief efforts, personally underwriting nearly a quarter of the aid sent aboard the _USS Constellation_ to Ireland. In 1897, he and his brother, Michael Grace, co-founded the _Grace Institute_—an enduring institution dedicated to the vocational education of women, particularly immigrants, in New York City.
On September 11, 1859, Grace married Lillius Gilchrist (1839–1922), daughter of George W. Gilchrist, a distinguished shipbuilder of Thomaston, Maine, and Mary Jane Smalley Gilchrist. Together, William and Lillius had eleven children, further cementing the Grace family’s legacy in both American public life and transatlantic history.
William Russell Grace died on March 21, 1904. His life and career encapsulate the story of 19th-century America itself—immigration, enterprise, public service, and philanthropy—and his legacy continues through the institutions he built and the ideals he championed.

**William R. Grace**was an American shipowner and founder of W.R. Grace & Co., a corporation that was for many years a dominant influence on the economy of South America’s west coast and, under the management of his heirs, became a multibillion-dollar conglomerate in the late 20th century.
Grace ran away to New York at the age of 14 but later returned to Ireland. In 1850 he visited Callao, Peru, where he entered the shipping house of Bryce & Co. as a clerk, becoming a partner two years later. Early success came to him when he positioned one of the firm’s supply ships off the Peruvian coast, thereby permitting cargo fleets to purchase supplies without sending their workers ashore. In 1854 the firm became Bryce, Grace & Co. and within a few years controlled much of the shipping along the coasts of Peru and Chile. His health declining, Grace turned the management of the firm over to his brother and left Peru in 1865.

# William R. Grace
In 1868 he organized the shipping firm of W.R. Grace & Co. in New York, serving ports on three continents and in the process winning a substantial portion of the U.S.–South American trade. Grace was the main arms supplier to Peru before and during its unsuccessful war with Chile in 1879–83, and after the war he assumed the country’s staggering war debt. In return, his company received huge concessions from Peru in the form of silver mines, oil and mineral deposits, and guano deposits. His business exploits in the country earned him the moniker “Pirate of Peru.” Grace also invested extensively in commodities and real estate in Peru and Chile and had numerous other business interests both in the United States and abroad. In 1892 he established the first direct steamship service between New York and Peru.
Grace was a major contributor to the Irish famine relief effort in 1880. He became interested in politics and was twice elected mayor of New York, in 1880 and 1884. His advocacy of a shipping canal through Central America met with success with the start of American-led construction of the Panama Canal in 1904.

## **William Russell Grace (1832–1904): Industrialist, Politician, and Philanthropist**
William Russell Grace stands as one of the most influential Irish-American figures of the 19th century—a pioneering industrialist, reformist mayor of New York City, and humanitarian of international renown. Born on May 10, 1832, in Riverstown near the Cove of Cork, Ireland, Grace was the son of James Grace and Eleanor May Russell (née Ellen). Though his birth occurred while the family was away from home, he was raised on the Grace estate at Ballylinan in Queen’s County (now County Laois), near the town of Athy. The family also resided for a time at Brooklawn House on Love Lane (now Donore Avenue), indicative of their prominent social standing.
In 1846, at the age of 14, young Grace defied his father's wishes and emigrated to New York City, where he labored as a printer’s devil and a shoemaker’s helper before briefly returning to Ireland in 1848. He later attended Belvedere College in Dublin but left before completing his studies.
In 1851, William and his father journeyed to Callao, Peru, with the ambitious aim of establishing an Irish agricultural colony. While James Grace returned to Ireland, William remained in Peru, where he entered the service of the shipping firm John Bryce & Co. His aptitude for commerce quickly became evident. The firm was restructured as Bryce, Grace & Company in 1854, and later as Grace Brothers & Co. in 1865. By the 1870s, it became _W. R. Grace and Company_, which would grow into a global enterprise with enduring influence in shipping, chemicals, and finance.

## **William Russell Grace (1832–1904): Industrialist, Politician, and Philanthropist**
Grace’s rise in the mercantile world was matched by a notable political career. In 1880, he made history as the first Roman Catholic—and the first Irish-American—to be elected mayor of New York City, running as an opponent of the corrupt Tammany Hall political machine. His administration was marked by a commitment to civic reform: he rooted out police corruption, curtailed patronage networks, cracked down on organized vice, and successfully opposed the Louisiana Lottery. Although defeated in the subsequent election, he returned triumphantly to office in 1884 on an Independent ticket. During his second term, Grace had the honor of formally receiving the Statue of Liberty from France, a symbolic moment in the city’s and nation’s immigrant narrative.
Outside of politics and business, Grace was an exemplary philanthropist. Following the Irish Famine of 1879, he played a leading role in relief efforts, personally underwriting nearly a quarter of the aid sent aboard the _USS Constellation_ to Ireland. In 1897, he and his brother, Michael Grace, co-founded the _Grace Institute_—an enduring institution dedicated to the vocational education of women, particularly immigrants, in New York City.
On September 11, 1859, Grace married Lillius Gilchrist (1839–1922), daughter of George W. Gilchrist, a distinguished shipbuilder of Thomaston, Maine, and Mary Jane Smalley Gilchrist. Together, William and Lillius had eleven children, further cementing the Grace family’s legacy in both American public life and transatlantic history.
William Russell Grace died on March 21, 1904. His life and career encapsulate the story of 19th-century America itself—immigration, enterprise, public service, and philanthropy—and his legacy continues through the institutions he built and the ideals he championed.

Grace, William Russell (1832–1904), international capitalist and mayor of New York City, was born 10 May 1832 in Riverstown, Co. Cork, while his family was on holiday, eldest son among four sons and three daughters of James Grace, farmer, and Ellen Mary Grace (née Russell), of Queen's Co. (Laois). Fascinated by the sea, despite growing up inland, he decided in 1846 to join the Royal Navy, but when this was vetoed by his father, he left school and worked his passage on a sailing vessel to New York, where he stayed for two years. When he returned to Ireland on a visit, his father persuaded him to remain in Europe, and he attended Belvedere College in Dublin briefly, before going to work in a Liverpool firm of ship chandlers. Disillusioned with his lack of opportunities, in 1850 he emigrated to Peru with his father, and they began working at a firm in Callao. With the assistance of his brother Michael, the firm expanded rapidly, evolving from Bryce & Co. to Bryce, Grace, & Co., eventually becoming (1854) Grace Brothers & Co. Initially exporting guano fertiliser from Peru to North America and Europe, the company soon diversified into other goods. In 1860 Grace was forced through ill-health to leave South America, and he travelled widely, visiting Ireland before returning to New York in 1865, where he established W. R. Grace & Co. to pursue a triangular trade between Europe and the Americas. Various brothers and relatives were enlisted to help run the new trading houses in Valparaiso, Callao, and other South American ports and cities.

Consolidating his massive economic interest in Peru, Grace secured for his companies a virtual monopoly on supplying the country's new railway system. He began to exert an increasing dominance in the country; his advice was regularly sought by the government, and for a time he was even responsible for equipping the Peruvian army (1875–9) and developing the navy. During Peru's unsuccessful ‘war of the Pacific’ with Chile (1879–83), Grace supplied the country with munitions and purchased additional ships for the navy. Although the war almost bankrupted Peru, Grace seized the opportunity to establish a controlling interest in the country's economy. Through the Grace contract of 1890 he took over the Peruvian national debt (over $250 million) in return for securing almost unlimited trading concessions. The company that had been established to administer these concessions, the Peruvian Corporation Ltd, was largely directed by Grace himself. By this manoeuvre Grace's fortune was assured: his company secured the silver mines of Cerro de Pasco; the complete output of the guano deposits; five million acres of land containing rich oil and mineral deposits; the right to construct, and hold in perpetuity, a national road; and a sixty-six-year lease on two railways.

Directing his developing multi-national from New York, with the sobriquet ‘the Pirate of Peru’, he was elected Democrat mayor of the city, the first Roman Catholic to hold that office (1880–82). He served a second term in 1884 as an independent, continuing his reform administration: reducing taxes; investigating police corruption, patronage, and other abuses of power; and breaking up the Louisiana Lottery in the city. Refusing a third term of office, in 1891 he established the New York & Pacific Steamship Co., and this later developed into the Grace Line, the first steamship line between the Americas, which reinforced his economic dominance in Latin America. Determined to expand outside Peru, he merged the two Grace companies under a Virginia charter (1895) as William R. Grace & Co., and established branches in almost every Latin American country. Nitrate mines and sugar mills were operated in Chile, tin was exported from Bolivia, and railroads were financed in Ecuador. In 1897 he founded the Grace Institute in New York to educate women in stenography, dressmaking, and housekeeping; a keen philanthropist, he gave his contributions mainly to the Roman Catholic church.
He married (11 Sept. 1859) Lillius Gilchrist, daughter of a shipbuilder; they had two sons and four daughters. He died 21 March 1904 in New York. W. R. Grace & Co. continued to trade after his death, operating Panaga, the leading air carrier between the Americas, from the 1930s to the 1950s, and continuing to control economic interests in Latin America, as the first multinational there. The company is largely credited with modernising the region but is also criticised for exploiting resources, repatriating profits, and interfering in host-country politics. In the 1950s the company sold its Latin American interests and concentrated its investments in the chemicals industry in the United States, where it remains a leading supplier.

texts.0: Grace, William Russell (1832–1904), international capitalist and mayor of New York City, was born 10 May 1832 in Riverstown, Co. Cork, while his family was on holiday, eldest son among four sons and three daughters of James Grace, farmer, and Ellen Mary Grace (née Russell), of Queen's Co. (Laois). Fascinated by the sea, despite growing up inland, he decided in 1846 to join the Royal Navy, but when this was vetoed by his father, he left school and worked his passage on a sailing vessel to New York, where he stayed for two years. When he returned to Ireland on a visit, his father persuaded him to remain in Europe, and he attended Belvedere College in Dublin briefly, before going to work in a Liverpool firm of ship chandlers. Disillusioned with his lack of opportunities, in 1850 he emigrated to Peru with his father, and they began working at a firm in Callao. With the assistance of his brother Michael, the firm expanded rapidly, evolving from Bryce & Co. to Bryce, Grace, & Co., eventually becoming (1854) Grace Brothers & Co. Initially exporting guano fertiliser from Peru to North America and Europe, the company soon diversified into other goods. In 1860 Grace was forced through ill-health to leave South America, and he travelled widely, visiting Ireland before returning to New York in 1865, where he established W. R. Grace & Co. to pursue a triangular trade between Europe and the Americas. Various brothers and relatives were enlisted to help run the new trading houses in Valparaiso, Callao, and other South American ports and cities.
texts.1: Consolidating his massive economic interest in Peru, Grace secured for his companies a virtual monopoly on supplying the country's new railway system. He began to exert an increasing dominance in the country; his advice was regularly sought by the government, and for a time he was even responsible for equipping the Peruvian army (1875–9) and developing the navy. During Peru's unsuccessful ‘war of the Pacific’ with Chile (1879–83), Grace supplied the country with munitions and purchased additional ships for the navy. Although the war almost bankrupted Peru, Grace seized the opportunity to establish a controlling interest in the country's economy. Through the Grace contract of 1890 he took over the Peruvian national debt (over $250 million) in return for securing almost unlimited trading concessions. The company that had been established to administer these concessions, the Peruvian Corporation Ltd, was largely directed by Grace himself. By this manoeuvre Grace's fortune was assured: his company secured the silver mines of Cerro de Pasco; the complete output of the guano deposits; five million acres of land containing rich oil and mineral deposits; the right to construct, and hold in perpetuity, a national road; and a sixty-six-year lease on two railways.
texts.2:
Directing his developing multi-national from New York, with the sobriquet ‘the Pirate of Peru’, he was elected Democrat mayor of the city, the first Roman Catholic to hold that office (1880–82). He served a second term in 1884 as an independent, continuing his reform administration: reducing taxes; investigating police corruption, patronage, and other abuses of power; and breaking up the Louisiana Lottery in the city. Refusing a third term of office, in 1891 he established the New York & Pacific Steamship Co., and this later developed into the Grace Line, the first steamship line between the Americas, which reinforced his economic dominance in Latin America. Determined to expand outside Peru, he merged the two Grace companies under a Virginia charter (1895) as William R. Grace & Co., and established branches in almost every Latin American country. Nitrate mines and sugar mills were operated in Chile, tin was exported from Bolivia, and railroads were financed in Ecuador. In 1897 he founded the Grace Institute in New York to educate women in stenography, dressmaking, and housekeeping; a keen philanthropist, he gave his contributions mainly to the Roman Catholic church.
He married (11 Sept. 1859) Lillius Gilchrist, daughter of a shipbuilder; they had two sons and four daughters. He died 21 March 1904 in New York. W. R. Grace & Co. continued to trade after his death, operating Panaga, the leading air carrier between the Americas, from the 1930s to the 1950s, and continuing to control economic interests in Latin America, as the first multinational there. The company is largely credited with modernising the region but is also criticised for exploiting resources, repatriating profits, and interfering in host-country politics. In the 1950s the company sold its Latin American interests and concentrated its investments in the chemicals industry in the United States, where it remains a leading supplier.

## **William Russell Grace (1832–1904): Industrialist, Politician, and Philanthropist**
William Russell Grace stands as one of the most influential Irish-American figures of the 19th century—a pioneering industrialist, reformist mayor of New York City, and humanitarian of international renown. Born on May 10, 1832, in Riverstown near the Cove of Cork, Ireland, Grace was the son of James Grace and Eleanor May Russell (née Ellen). Though his birth occurred while the family was away from home, he was raised on the Grace estate at Ballylinan in Queen’s County (now County Laois), near the town of Athy. The family also resided for a time at Brooklawn House on Love Lane (now Donore Avenue), indicative of their prominent social standing.
In 1846, at the age of 14, young Grace defied his father's wishes and emigrated to New York City, where he labored as a printer’s devil and a shoemaker’s helper before briefly returning to Ireland in 1848. He later attended Belvedere College in Dublin but left before completing his studies.
In 1851, William and his father journeyed to Callao, Peru, with the ambitious aim of establishing an Irish agricultural colony. While James Grace returned to Ireland, William remained in Peru, where he entered the service of the shipping firm John Bryce & Co. His aptitude for commerce quickly became evident. The firm was restructured as Bryce, Grace & Company in 1854, and later as Grace Brothers & Co. in 1865. By the 1870s, it became _W. R. Grace and Company_, which would grow into a global enterprise with enduring influence in shipping, chemicals, and finance.

## **William Russell Grace (1832–1904): Industrialist, Politician, and Philanthropist**
Grace’s rise in the mercantile world was matched by a notable political career. In 1880, he made history as the first Roman Catholic—and the first Irish-American—to be elected mayor of New York City, running as an opponent of the corrupt Tammany Hall political machine. His administration was marked by a commitment to civic reform: he rooted out police corruption, curtailed patronage networks, cracked down on organized vice, and successfully opposed the Louisiana Lottery. Although defeated in the subsequent election, he returned triumphantly to office in 1884 on an Independent ticket. During his second term, Grace had the honor of formally receiving the Statue of Liberty from France, a symbolic moment in the city’s and nation’s immigrant narrative.
Outside of politics and business, Grace was an exemplary philanthropist. Following the Irish Famine of 1879, he played a leading role in relief efforts, personally underwriting nearly a quarter of the aid sent aboard the _USS Constellation_ to Ireland. In 1897, he and his brother, Michael Grace, co-founded the _Grace Institute_—an enduring institution dedicated to the vocational education of women, particularly immigrants, in New York City.
On September 11, 1859, Grace married Lillius Gilchrist (1839–1922), daughter of George W. Gilchrist, a distinguished shipbuilder of Thomaston, Maine, and Mary Jane Smalley Gilchrist. Together, William and Lillius had eleven children, further cementing the Grace family’s legacy in both American public life and transatlantic history.
William Russell Grace died on March 21, 1904. His life and career encapsulate the story of 19th-century America itself—immigration, enterprise, public service, and philanthropy—and his legacy continues through the institutions he built and the ideals he championed.

Grace, William Russell (1832–1904), international capitalist and mayor of New York City, was born 10 May 1832 in Riverstown, Co. Cork, while his family was on holiday, eldest son among four sons and three daughters of James Grace, farmer, and Ellen Mary Grace (née Russell), of Queen's Co. (Laois). Fascinated by the sea, despite growing up inland, he decided in 1846 to join the Royal Navy, but when this was vetoed by his father, he left school and worked his passage on a sailing vessel to New York, where he stayed for two years. When he returned to Ireland on a visit, his father persuaded him to remain in Europe, and he attended Belvedere College in Dublin briefly, before going to work in a Liverpool firm of ship chandlers. Disillusioned with his lack of opportunities, in 1850 he emigrated to Peru with his father, and they began working at a firm in Callao. With the assistance of his brother Michael, the firm expanded rapidly, evolving from Bryce & Co. to Bryce, Grace, & Co., eventually becoming (1854) Grace Brothers & Co. Initially exporting guano fertiliser from Peru to North America and Europe, the company soon diversified into other goods. In 1860 Grace was forced through ill-health to leave South America, and he travelled widely, visiting Ireland before returning to New York in 1865, where he established W. R. Grace & Co. to pursue a triangular trade between Europe and the Americas. Various brothers and relatives were enlisted to help run the new trading houses in Valparaiso, Callao, and other South American ports and cities.

Consolidating his massive economic interest in Peru, Grace secured for his companies a virtual monopoly on supplying the country's new railway system. He began to exert an increasing dominance in the country; his advice was regularly sought by the government, and for a time he was even responsible for equipping the Peruvian army (1875–9) and developing the navy. During Peru's unsuccessful ‘war of the Pacific’ with Chile (1879–83), Grace supplied the country with munitions and purchased additional ships for the navy. Although the war almost bankrupted Peru, Grace seized the opportunity to establish a controlling interest in the country's economy. Through the Grace contract of 1890 he took over the Peruvian national debt (over $250 million) in return for securing almost unlimited trading concessions. The company that had been established to administer these concessions, the Peruvian Corporation Ltd, was largely directed by Grace himself. By this manoeuvre Grace's fortune was assured: his company secured the silver mines of Cerro de Pasco; the complete output of the guano deposits; five million acres of land containing rich oil and mineral deposits; the right to construct, and hold in perpetuity, a national road; and a sixty-six-year lease on two railways.

Directing his developing multi-national from New York, with the sobriquet ‘the Pirate of Peru’, he was elected Democrat mayor of the city, the first Roman Catholic to hold that office (1880–82). He served a second term in 1884 as an independent, continuing his reform administration: reducing taxes; investigating police corruption, patronage, and other abuses of power; and breaking up the Louisiana Lottery in the city. Refusing a third term of office, in 1891 he established the New York & Pacific Steamship Co., and this later developed into the Grace Line, the first steamship line between the Americas, which reinforced his economic dominance in Latin America. Determined to expand outside Peru, he merged the two Grace companies under a Virginia charter (1895) as William R. Grace & Co., and established branches in almost every Latin American country. Nitrate mines and sugar mills were operated in Chile, tin was exported from Bolivia, and railroads were financed in Ecuador. In 1897 he founded the Grace Institute in New York to educate women in stenography, dressmaking, and housekeeping; a keen philanthropist, he gave his contributions mainly to the Roman Catholic church.
He married (11 Sept. 1859) Lillius Gilchrist, daughter of a shipbuilder; they had two sons and four daughters. He died 21 March 1904 in New York. W. R. Grace & Co. continued to trade after his death, operating Panaga, the leading air carrier between the Americas, from the 1930s to the 1950s, and continuing to control economic interests in Latin America, as the first multinational there. The company is largely credited with modernising the region but is also criticised for exploiting resources, repatriating profits, and interfering in host-country politics. In the 1950s the company sold its Latin American interests and concentrated its investments in the chemicals industry in the United States, where it remains a leading supplier.

**William R. Grace**was an American shipowner and founder of W.R. Grace & Co., a corporation that was for many years a dominant influence on the economy of South America’s west coast and, under the management of his heirs, became a multibillion-dollar conglomerate in the late 20th century.
Grace ran away to New York at the age of 14 but later returned to Ireland. In 1850 he visited Callao, Peru, where he entered the shipping house of Bryce & Co. as a clerk, becoming a partner two years later. Early success came to him when he positioned one of the firm’s supply ships off the Peruvian coast, thereby permitting cargo fleets to purchase supplies without sending their workers ashore. In 1854 the firm became Bryce, Grace & Co. and within a few years controlled much of the shipping along the coasts of Peru and Chile. His health declining, Grace turned the management of the firm over to his brother and left Peru in 1865.

# William R. Grace
In 1868 he organized the shipping firm of W.R. Grace & Co. in New York, serving ports on three continents and in the process winning a substantial portion of the U.S.–South American trade. Grace was the main arms supplier to Peru before and during its unsuccessful war with Chile in 1879–83, and after the war he assumed the country’s staggering war debt. In return, his company received huge concessions from Peru in the form of silver mines, oil and mineral deposits, and guano deposits. His business exploits in the country earned him the moniker “Pirate of Peru.” Grace also invested extensively in commodities and real estate in Peru and Chile and had numerous other business interests both in the United States and abroad. In 1892 he established the first direct steamship service between New York and Peru.
Grace was a major contributor to the Irish famine relief effort in 1880. He became interested in politics and was twice elected mayor of New York, in 1880 and 1884. His advocacy of a shipping canal through Central America met with success with the start of American-led construction of the Panama Canal in 1904.

# William R. Grace
In 1868 he organized the shipping firm of W.R. Grace & Co. in New York, serving ports on three continents and in the process winning a substantial portion of the U.S.–South American trade. Grace was the main arms supplier to Peru before and during its unsuccessful war with Chile in 1879–83, and after the war he assumed the country’s staggering war debt. In return, his company received huge concessions from Peru in the form of silver mines, oil and mineral deposits, and guano deposits. His business exploits in the country earned him the moniker “Pirate of Peru.” Grace also invested extensively in commodities and real estate in Peru and Chile and had numerous other business interests both in the United States and abroad. In 1892 he established the first direct steamship service between New York and Peru.
Grace was a major contributor to the Irish famine relief effort in 1880. He became interested in politics and was twice elected mayor of New York, in 1880 and 1884. His advocacy of a shipping canal through Central America met with success with the start of American-led construction of the Panama Canal in 1904.

## **William Russell Grace (1832–1904): Industrialist, Politician, and Philanthropist**
William Russell Grace stands as one of the most influential Irish-American figures of the 19th century—a pioneering industrialist, reformist mayor of New York City, and humanitarian of international renown. Born on May 10, 1832, in Riverstown near the Cove of Cork, Ireland, Grace was the son of James Grace and Eleanor May Russell (née Ellen). Though his birth occurred while the family was away from home, he was raised on the Grace estate at Ballylinan in Queen’s County (now County Laois), near the town of Athy. The family also resided for a time at Brooklawn House on Love Lane (now Donore Avenue), indicative of their prominent social standing.
In 1846, at the age of 14, young Grace defied his father's wishes and emigrated to New York City, where he labored as a printer’s devil and a shoemaker’s helper before briefly returning to Ireland in 1848. He later attended Belvedere College in Dublin but left before completing his studies.
In 1851, William and his father journeyed to Callao, Peru, with the ambitious aim of establishing an Irish agricultural colony. While James Grace returned to Ireland, William remained in Peru, where he entered the service of the shipping firm John Bryce & Co. His aptitude for commerce quickly became evident. The firm was restructured as Bryce, Grace & Company in 1854, and later as Grace Brothers & Co. in 1865. By the 1870s, it became _W. R. Grace and Company_, which would grow into a global enterprise with enduring influence in shipping, chemicals, and finance.

## **William Russell Grace (1832–1904): Industrialist, Politician, and Philanthropist**
Grace’s rise in the mercantile world was matched by a notable political career. In 1880, he made history as the first Roman Catholic—and the first Irish-American—to be elected mayor of New York City, running as an opponent of the corrupt Tammany Hall political machine. His administration was marked by a commitment to civic reform: he rooted out police corruption, curtailed patronage networks, cracked down on organized vice, and successfully opposed the Louisiana Lottery. Although defeated in the subsequent election, he returned triumphantly to office in 1884 on an Independent ticket. During his second term, Grace had the honor of formally receiving the Statue of Liberty from France, a symbolic moment in the city’s and nation’s immigrant narrative.
Outside of politics and business, Grace was an exemplary philanthropist. Following the Irish Famine of 1879, he played a leading role in relief efforts, personally underwriting nearly a quarter of the aid sent aboard the _USS Constellation_ to Ireland. In 1897, he and his brother, Michael Grace, co-founded the _Grace Institute_—an enduring institution dedicated to the vocational education of women, particularly immigrants, in New York City.
On September 11, 1859, Grace married Lillius Gilchrist (1839–1922), daughter of George W. Gilchrist, a distinguished shipbuilder of Thomaston, Maine, and Mary Jane Smalley Gilchrist. Together, William and Lillius had eleven children, further cementing the Grace family’s legacy in both American public life and transatlantic history.
William Russell Grace died on March 21, 1904. His life and career encapsulate the story of 19th-century America itself—immigration, enterprise, public service, and philanthropy—and his legacy continues through the institutions he built and the ideals he championed.

**William R. Grace**was an American shipowner and founder of W.R. Grace & Co., a corporation that was for many years a dominant influence on the economy of South America’s west coast and, under the management of his heirs, became a multibillion-dollar conglomerate in the late 20th century.
Grace ran away to New York at the age of 14 but later returned to Ireland. In 1850 he visited Callao, Peru, where he entered the shipping house of Bryce & Co. as a clerk, becoming a partner two years later. Early success came to him when he positioned one of the firm’s supply ships off the Peruvian coast, thereby permitting cargo fleets to purchase supplies without sending their workers ashore. In 1854 the firm became Bryce, Grace & Co. and within a few years controlled much of the shipping along the coasts of Peru and Chile. His health declining, Grace turned the management of the firm over to his brother and left Peru in 1865.

# William R. Grace
In 1868 he organized the shipping firm of W.R. Grace & Co. in New York, serving ports on three continents and in the process winning a substantial portion of the U.S.–South American trade. Grace was the main arms supplier to Peru before and during its unsuccessful war with Chile in 1879–83, and after the war he assumed the country’s staggering war debt. In return, his company received huge concessions from Peru in the form of silver mines, oil and mineral deposits, and guano deposits. His business exploits in the country earned him the moniker “Pirate of Peru.” Grace also invested extensively in commodities and real estate in Peru and Chile and had numerous other business interests both in the United States and abroad. In 1892 he established the first direct steamship service between New York and Peru.
Grace was a major contributor to the Irish famine relief effort in 1880. He became interested in politics and was twice elected mayor of New York, in 1880 and 1884. His advocacy of a shipping canal through Central America met with success with the start of American-led construction of the Panama Canal in 1904.

**William R. Grace**was an American shipowner and founder of W.R. Grace & Co., a corporation that was for many years a dominant influence on the economy of South America’s west coast and, under the management of his heirs, became a multibillion-dollar conglomerate in the late 20th century.
Grace ran away to New York at the age of 14 but later returned to Ireland. In 1850 he visited Callao, Peru, where he entered the shipping house of Bryce & Co. as a clerk, becoming a partner two years later. Early success came to him when he positioned one of the firm’s supply ships off the Peruvian coast, thereby permitting cargo fleets to purchase supplies without sending their workers ashore. In 1854 the firm became Bryce, Grace & Co. and within a few years controlled much of the shipping along the coasts of Peru and Chile. His health declining, Grace turned the management of the firm over to his brother and left Peru in 1865.

# William R. Grace
In 1868 he organized the shipping firm of W.R. Grace & Co. in New York, serving ports on three continents and in the process winning a substantial portion of the U.S.–South American trade. Grace was the main arms supplier to Peru before and during its unsuccessful war with Chile in 1879–83, and after the war he assumed the country’s staggering war debt. In return, his company received huge concessions from Peru in the form of silver mines, oil and mineral deposits, and guano deposits. His business exploits in the country earned him the moniker “Pirate of Peru.” Grace also invested extensively in commodities and real estate in Peru and Chile and had numerous other business interests both in the United States and abroad. In 1892 he established the first direct steamship service between New York and Peru.
Grace was a major contributor to the Irish famine relief effort in 1880. He became interested in politics and was twice elected mayor of New York, in 1880 and 1884. His advocacy of a shipping canal through Central America met with success with the start of American-led construction of the Panama Canal in 1904.

## **William Russell Grace (1832–1904): Industrialist, Politician, and Philanthropist**
William Russell Grace stands as one of the most influential Irish-American figures of the 19th century—a pioneering industrialist, reformist mayor of New York City, and humanitarian of international renown. Born on May 10, 1832, in Riverstown near the Cove of Cork, Ireland, Grace was the son of James Grace and Eleanor May Russell (née Ellen). Though his birth occurred while the family was away from home, he was raised on the Grace estate at Ballylinan in Queen’s County (now County Laois), near the town of Athy. The family also resided for a time at Brooklawn House on Love Lane (now Donore Avenue), indicative of their prominent social standing.
In 1846, at the age of 14, young Grace defied his father's wishes and emigrated to New York City, where he labored as a printer’s devil and a shoemaker’s helper before briefly returning to Ireland in 1848. He later attended Belvedere College in Dublin but left before completing his studies.
In 1851, William and his father journeyed to Callao, Peru, with the ambitious aim of establishing an Irish agricultural colony. While James Grace returned to Ireland, William remained in Peru, where he entered the service of the shipping firm John Bryce & Co. His aptitude for commerce quickly became evident. The firm was restructured as Bryce, Grace & Company in 1854, and later as Grace Brothers & Co. in 1865. By the 1870s, it became _W. R. Grace and Company_, which would grow into a global enterprise with enduring influence in shipping, chemicals, and finance.

## **William Russell Grace (1832–1904): Industrialist, Politician, and Philanthropist**
Grace’s rise in the mercantile world was matched by a notable political career. In 1880, he made history as the first Roman Catholic—and the first Irish-American—to be elected mayor of New York City, running as an opponent of the corrupt Tammany Hall political machine. His administration was marked by a commitment to civic reform: he rooted out police corruption, curtailed patronage networks, cracked down on organized vice, and successfully opposed the Louisiana Lottery. Although defeated in the subsequent election, he returned triumphantly to office in 1884 on an Independent ticket. During his second term, Grace had the honor of formally receiving the Statue of Liberty from France, a symbolic moment in the city’s and nation’s immigrant narrative.
Outside of politics and business, Grace was an exemplary philanthropist. Following the Irish Famine of 1879, he played a leading role in relief efforts, personally underwriting nearly a quarter of the aid sent aboard the _USS Constellation_ to Ireland. In 1897, he and his brother, Michael Grace, co-founded the _Grace Institute_—an enduring institution dedicated to the vocational education of women, particularly immigrants, in New York City.
On September 11, 1859, Grace married Lillius Gilchrist (1839–1922), daughter of George W. Gilchrist, a distinguished shipbuilder of Thomaston, Maine, and Mary Jane Smalley Gilchrist. Together, William and Lillius had eleven children, further cementing the Grace family’s legacy in both American public life and transatlantic history.
William Russell Grace died on March 21, 1904. His life and career encapsulate the story of 19th-century America itself—immigration, enterprise, public service, and philanthropy—and his legacy continues through the institutions he built and the ideals he championed.

**William R. Grace**was an American shipowner and founder of W.R. Grace & Co., a corporation that was for many years a dominant influence on the economy of South America’s west coast and, under the management of his heirs, became a multibillion-dollar conglomerate in the late 20th century.
Grace ran away to New York at the age of 14 but later returned to Ireland. In 1850 he visited Callao, Peru, where he entered the shipping house of Bryce & Co. as a clerk, becoming a partner two years later. Early success came to him when he positioned one of the firm’s supply ships off the Peruvian coast, thereby permitting cargo fleets to purchase supplies without sending their workers ashore. In 1854 the firm became Bryce, Grace & Co. and within a few years controlled much of the shipping along the coasts of Peru and Chile. His health declining, Grace turned the management of the firm over to his brother and left Peru in 1865.

# William R. Grace
In 1868 he organized the shipping firm of W.R. Grace & Co. in New York, serving ports on three continents and in the process winning a substantial portion of the U.S.–South American trade. Grace was the main arms supplier to Peru before and during its unsuccessful war with Chile in 1879–83, and after the war he assumed the country’s staggering war debt. In return, his company received huge concessions from Peru in the form of silver mines, oil and mineral deposits, and guano deposits. His business exploits in the country earned him the moniker “Pirate of Peru.” Grace also invested extensively in commodities and real estate in Peru and Chile and had numerous other business interests both in the United States and abroad. In 1892 he established the first direct steamship service between New York and Peru.
Grace was a major contributor to the Irish famine relief effort in 1880. He became interested in politics and was twice elected mayor of New York, in 1880 and 1884. His advocacy of a shipping canal through Central America met with success with the start of American-led construction of the Panama Canal in 1904.

## **William Russell Grace (1832–1904): Industrialist, Politician, and Philanthropist**
William Russell Grace stands as one of the most influential Irish-American figures of the 19th century—a pioneering industrialist, reformist mayor of New York City, and humanitarian of international renown. Born on May 10, 1832, in Riverstown near the Cove of Cork, Ireland, Grace was the son of James Grace and Eleanor May Russell (née Ellen). Though his birth occurred while the family was away from home, he was raised on the Grace estate at Ballylinan in Queen’s County (now County Laois), near the town of Athy. The family also resided for a time at Brooklawn House on Love Lane (now Donore Avenue), indicative of their prominent social standing.
In 1846, at the age of 14, young Grace defied his father's wishes and emigrated to New York City, where he labored as a printer’s devil and a shoemaker’s helper before briefly returning to Ireland in 1848. He later attended Belvedere College in Dublin but left before completing his studies.
In 1851, William and his father journeyed to Callao, Peru, with the ambitious aim of establishing an Irish agricultural colony. While James Grace returned to Ireland, William remained in Peru, where he entered the service of the shipping firm John Bryce & Co. His aptitude for commerce quickly became evident. The firm was restructured as Bryce, Grace & Company in 1854, and later as Grace Brothers & Co. in 1865. By the 1870s, it became _W. R. Grace and Company_, which would grow into a global enterprise with enduring influence in shipping, chemicals, and finance.

## **William Russell Grace (1832–1904): Industrialist, Politician, and Philanthropist**
Grace’s rise in the mercantile world was matched by a notable political career. In 1880, he made history as the first Roman Catholic—and the first Irish-American—to be elected mayor of New York City, running as an opponent of the corrupt Tammany Hall political machine. His administration was marked by a commitment to civic reform: he rooted out police corruption, curtailed patronage networks, cracked down on organized vice, and successfully opposed the Louisiana Lottery. Although defeated in the subsequent election, he returned triumphantly to office in 1884 on an Independent ticket. During his second term, Grace had the honor of formally receiving the Statue of Liberty from France, a symbolic moment in the city’s and nation’s immigrant narrative.
Outside of politics and business, Grace was an exemplary philanthropist. Following the Irish Famine of 1879, he played a leading role in relief efforts, personally underwriting nearly a quarter of the aid sent aboard the _USS Constellation_ to Ireland. In 1897, he and his brother, Michael Grace, co-founded the _Grace Institute_—an enduring institution dedicated to the vocational education of women, particularly immigrants, in New York City.
On September 11, 1859, Grace married Lillius Gilchrist (1839–1922), daughter of George W. Gilchrist, a distinguished shipbuilder of Thomaston, Maine, and Mary Jane Smalley Gilchrist. Together, William and Lillius had eleven children, further cementing the Grace family’s legacy in both American public life and transatlantic history.
William Russell Grace died on March 21, 1904. His life and career encapsulate the story of 19th-century America itself—immigration, enterprise, public service, and philanthropy—and his legacy continues through the institutions he built and the ideals he championed.
